items.abstract: <jats:p>Financial fraud today moves faster than the annual or quarterly review cycles that most detection systems were designed around. A stolen card can be tested across dozens of merchants and monetized within minutes, and a compromised account can be drained before a human analyst ever opens a case. Detection systems built as a single model or a single rules engine struggle here, not because the underlying machine learning is weak, but because a single system covers too many kinds of fraud with too few, and too tightly coupled, sources of evidence. This paper proposes a parent-child multi-agent architecture for real-time fraud detection, in which a coordinating parent agent routes each transaction to a small set of specialized child agents, each bound to its own tools and data sources through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). We ground the design in the current literature on large language model multi-agent systems, agent-tool interoperability, and graph-based fraud detection, and we present the architecture, a reference implementation pattern, six representative use cases, and a qualitative comparison against rule-based, single-model, and monolithic-agent baselines. The contribution is architectural rather than empirical: we do not report benchmark numbers, but we give practitioners and researchers a concrete, citable design they can implement, adapt, and evaluate against their own transaction data.</jats:p>
title: A Parent-Child Multi-Agent Architecture for Real-Time Financial Fraud Detection Using Tool-Augmented Language Model Agents
